prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize for optical lattice clocks to Katori and Ye. I moved to it from IceCube at the opening stage and the round-1 exchange has not given me a reason to move back. The scientific case rests on a specific idea, Katori's magic-wavelength lattice, which cancels the light shift so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. It was followed by a decisive first demonstration and then by a long campaign on blackbody, hyperpolarisability and collisional systematics that took fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18, with Ye's group driving the record accuracy and the many-body and spin-exchange regime. Independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) now reproduce and intercompare these clocks, which is the test I always ask first of a claimed advance: has someone else confirmed it, and did the named contribution decide the outcome. The answer is yes on both counts for these two names. The instrument is already in use for tests of constants, gravitational redshift inside a single cloud and dark-matter searches. I am treating the breadth of support in round 1 as a reason to examine the case harder, not as evidence for it, and the case holds up when examined.
statement.case_against: The objection that carries the most weight, and that Eva Lindroth and Ulf Danielsson both raised in different words, is that this is invention and measurement more than surprise, building on the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize. I am an instrument builder and I know my pull toward precision for its own sake, so I have tried to test the case against a stricter standard. My answer is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a distinct concept from both earlier prizes: combs count optical cycles, ion control isolates a single quantum system, and the lattice clock solves the separate problem of holding a large ensemble without perturbing the transition. The remaining weaknesses are real. The SI second has not yet been redefined. Ion clocks (Al+, Yb+) reach similar accuracy, so the citation must not imply that lattice clocks alone define the state of the art. And Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko and the many-body clock work sit outside the credited pair, with Ye's own position partly resting on combs and ultrastable cavities built by others. The B014 case is the strongest rival in discovery terms, but its credit problem is unresolved and I would not trade a defensible attribution for a better story.

responses.point: Ulf still prefers B014 as a sole prize, framed around the diffuse flux and neutrino astronomy rather than source identification, accepting that attribution to Halzen and Karle is the weak point and that B015 may be the easier choice to defend.
responses.response: I agree with his framing: if B014 were chosen, the citation should rest on the diffuse astrophysical flux and the opening of the field, not on TXS 0506+056. That is also my own instrument-builder's reading, because the flux is seen in several event channels and is the stable core. But the chair's question was whether the preference survives the attribution objections, and his own case_against concedes that two names understate AMANDA, DUMAND, Baikal, ANTARES and a collaboration of hundreds. I cannot see a three-name cut that fixes this without a clear record of who made the decisive detector choices, and the round-1 statements do not supply one. I therefore keep B014 as my first alternative, and I would not object if Ulf and the committee later find a citation that credits the detector concept narrowly.

responses.point: Olle prefers B003 (Kane, Molenkamp, Xue) as a complete theory-experiment arc with fifteen years of independent confirmation, accepts that Mele, Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal are omitted, and says B015 is the cleaner attribution case without having settled the choice.
responses.response: I accept that B003 is a mature, reproduced discovery of a new kind of matter, which is a different and in some ways weightier kind of achievement than a clock. His point that Xue's quantized anomalous Hall transport is the strongest proof that the topology is real is persuasive to me as an experimentalist. But the three-name cut still bundles two experiments by different groups, and he himself calls the attribution contestable with Mele and Hasan outside it. As a non-specialist I rely on him for the condensed-matter judgment, so I would ask him directly whether Kane and Molenkamp alone, or the B018 cut, is more defensible in his view. On the 2016 overlap I defer to him and Bernhard Mehlig that it is limited. I keep B003 as my second alternative, and I would support it if the committee finds the B015 case does not survive the questions below.

responses.point: Eva supports B015, admits it is invention and measurement more than surprise, warns that the citation must not imply lattice clocks alone define timekeeping because ion clocks compete, and notes that Lemonde and many-body work lie outside the credited names.
responses.response: Her platform-neutrality warning is the right constraint and I have built it into the citation. It names the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength principle, and says the clock reached 10^-18, not that it is the only clock to do so. On Lemonde and Takamoto, the boundary I would defend is that Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstration, while Ye took it to the accuracy regime and exploited many-body effects. Others made real contributions, but the three-name limit and the requirement that the credited contribution be decisive point to these two. I would welcome her checking the priority question between Katori's proposal and the first Sr lattice demonstrations, since she flagged she has not independently verified it.

responses.point: Stefan puts B015 first as the most precise instruments ever built, with clear systematics budgets, independent confirmation and a clean two-laureate configuration, and he flags his year in John Hall's laboratory as a possible link to Ye's milieu.
responses.response: On the chair's conflict question, I do not think his time in Hall's laboratory during his PhD is a reason to exclude him from the B015 deliberation. He reports no collaboration with Katori or Ye, and his experience of what a systematics budget actually involves is useful to the discussion. I would ask that the record show the disclosure and that the committee confirm it is content. On substance, his point about the SI second matters to timing, but I would not make the prize depend on a metrology-body decision: the scientific case stands on the reproduced 10^-18 results, and a redefinition would confirm the importance of the work and not create it.

uncertainties: Whether a citation can keep B015 clearly distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and I have tried to do so by naming the magic-wavelength lattice.
Whether the pending redefinition of the SI second argues for acting now or for waiting. My view is that it does not decide the matter, but I cannot rule out that colleagues weigh it differently.
Whether Lemonde, Takamoto and the ion-clock leaders should alter the credited pair. I do not have the first-hand record to settle this and rely on the atomic physicists.
How to credit B014 fairly among Halzen, Karle, the AMANDA lineage and a large collaboration, if the committee returns to it.
Whether B003 is best cut as Kane, Molenkamp and Xue, as Kane and Molenkamp alone, or as the B018 four-name version, which I cannot judge as a non-specialist.
statement.conflict_note: I am a member of the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, which places me in the same broad astroparticle community as B014 (IceCube) and to a lesser extent B045. I have no known personal or institutional link to any credited person on any shortlisted candidate, and none to Katori or Ye. I would recuse myself from chairing the deliberation on B014 if it became the leading candidate. Disclosures by others, in particular Kroll's time in Hall's laboratory and Johansson's possible recusal on B039, do not in my view prevent anyone from taking part in the B015 discussion, though I would like the committee to confirm that.
